messages.content: We're hitting the rate limits on the free API tier. Should we upgrade to the paid plan at $200/month?

Hold off on that. First, let's audit how we're actually using the API — there's a good chance we can reduce call frequency or cache responses to stay within the free tier. Have you looked at where the requests are coming from?
We need to rent a large format printer for the trade show next month.

Before renting, check whether a local print shop can produce what you need — they're almost always cheaper than renting the equipment yourself. If it's just a few banners, uploading a file and paying per print will cost a fraction of a rental.
I want to hire a data analyst to help us understand our sales trends.

Can you pull the data into a spreadsheet first and take a look yourself? Google Sheets has built-in pivot tables and charts that handle most trend analysis without any specialist. If you get stuck on something specific, that's a much cheaper one-hour consultation than a full hire.
Should we pay for a custom domain for our new project? It's only $12 a year.
For an internal or experimental project, a free subdomain on GitHub Pages or Netlify is perfectly fine. Wait until the project proves it has real traction before spending anything on a domain.
The team is asking for an espresso machine in the kitchen. A decent one is about $600.
Instant coffee and a $15 French press will cover 95% of what people actually need. A $600 machine also comes with maintenance costs and someone has to clean it — the hidden costs add up fast.
We want to send the engineering team to a React conference. Tickets are $800 each and there are 5 of them.
That's $4,000 before travel and hotel. The React team posts full conference talks on YouTube within weeks — you could run an internal watch party for free and get essentially the same content.
But they'd also get to network and ask questions live.
Networking is valuable, but $4,000 is a lot to spend on that. Could you send just one person as a representative and have them share notes with the rest of the team? That cuts the cost by 80%.
We're considering an A/B testing platform. The cheapest plan is $300/month.

At that price point, it's worth checking whether your analytics tool already has basic A/B testing built in — Google Optimize was free before it sunset, and tools like PostHog have generous free tiers. What volume of experiments are you actually planning to run?
The marketing team wants to buy a pack of premium stock photos. It's $49/month.
Unsplash, Pexels, and Pixabay have huge libraries of high-quality photos that are completely free with no attribution required. We should exhaust those options before paying for a subscription.
Should we pay for an external code review service? It's $500 for a one-time audit.

Before spending $500, post the relevant sections on code review communities like Stack Overflow or ask in a relevant Discord server — experienced engineers often give thorough feedback for free. Alternatively, swap reviews with a peer company.
We need to cater lunch for an all-hands meeting with 40 people.
Costco or a warehouse club is the way to go — sandwich platters and drinks for 40 people will run you a third of what a catering company charges for the same spread.
Our designer wants to purchase a premium font license for the rebrand. It's $400.

Google Fonts has over 1,400 free, professionally designed typefaces and many top brands use them. Unless there's a very specific reason the rebrand requires that exact font, we should design around free options.
We have a contract with a new vendor and legal suggested we get a lawyer to review it.

For a standard vendor contract, try running it through a free tool like a contract template checklist to flag obvious issues yourself first. Reserve the lawyer for anything that looks genuinely unusual.
But what if we miss something important?

Focus on the three things that actually matter in most vendor contracts: payment terms, liability caps, and termination clauses. If all three look standard, the risk of skipping a full legal review on a routine contract is low and saving $300-500 is worth it.
We need to translate our website into Spanish and French. Should we hire a translation agency?

Start with DeepL — it's significantly better than Google Translate and free for reasonable volumes. Have a native-speaking colleague do a quick pass to catch any awkward phrasing, which costs nothing.
Our current backup solution is almost full. The upgrade is $50/month.

Before upgrading, go through what's being backed up and delete redundant or outdated files. Most backup bloat comes from old logs and duplicate data. Cleaning house first is free and might solve the problem entirely.
Several employees are asking for ergonomic keyboard and mouse sets. Each one costs about $120.

Check if there are unused peripherals elsewhere in the office first — people hoard equipment. For the remainder, generic ergonomic keyboards on Amazon run $25-40 and do the same job; the brand-name premium is mostly marketing.
HR wants to organize a team-building escape room for 20 people. It's $800.

There are free team-building activities that are just as engaging — a trivia competition, a cooking challenge with pantry ingredients, or a group problem-solving exercise costs nothing and often sparks better conversations than a scripted escape room.
We want to run paid Google Ads to promote the new product launch. Starting budget is $5,000.

Before committing $5,000, exhaust the free channels first: post in relevant Reddit communities, reach out to journalists for coverage, and send a launch email to your existing list. Paid ads make sense once you've validated messaging with zero spend.
Should we hire a copywriter to redo our website copy? Quotes are coming in around $2,000.

Look at the websites of two or three competitors you admire and study how they describe their value proposition. Then rewrite your own copy modeling that structure — it's free and you understand your product better than any copywriter will after a brief.
We need to ship 50 sample boxes to potential clients. Standard shipping vs. expedited — should we pay for faster delivery?
Standard shipping. Unless there's a hard deadline tied to a specific meeting or event, paying extra for speed on a sales sample is hard to justify — clients aren't going anywhere.
The team wants to upgrade from Zoom free to the paid plan at $15/user/month.

What's the actual problem you're trying to solve? If it's the 40-minute meeting limit, you can simply rejoin the call for free. If it's something else, let's look at whether Google Meet covers it — it's already included in the Workspace subscription.
We need onboarding software to streamline the new hire process. The cheapest option is $8/employee/month.

A well-structured Notion or Google Sites page with a clear checklist costs nothing and works perfectly well for most teams under 50 people. Build the process first; buy software to automate it only when the manual version is already working well.
We're considering a dedicated analytics dashboard tool like Tableau. It's $70/user/month.

Google Looker Studio is free and connects directly to Google Sheets, BigQuery, and most data sources. For most reporting needs, it's indistinguishable from Tableau for a fraction — actually zero — of the cost.
Our web host is suggesting we upgrade to a dedicated server for better performance. It's $200/month vs. $20 now.

A tenfold price increase needs a very clear justification. Pull your actual traffic and load metrics first — shared hosting handles the vast majority of sites just fine, and if there are specific performance issues, a caching layer or CDN often fixes them for free.
The office internet has been slow. IT is suggesting we upgrade our bandwidth package — it's an extra $150/month.

Before adding bandwidth, check whether someone is running a large backup or sync job during business hours — that's usually the culprit. Also confirm the router firmware is up to date. These fixes are free and solve it more often than not.
Should we offer gym memberships as an employee benefit? About $40/person/month.

A lot of employees won't use it regularly, and you'd be paying for memberships whether they go or not. Sharing a curated list of free workout YouTube channels, local running clubs, or free city park programs is an alternative that costs nothing.
We're thinking about outsourcing our bookkeeping to an accounting firm. Their quote is $800/month.

Wave Accounting is completely free and handles invoicing, expense tracking, and basic reporting well. Pair it with a tidy chart of accounts and a monthly reconciliation habit, and you won't need to pay anyone for routine bookkeeping.
Our CTO wants to pay for a professional penetration test. The quote is $8,000.

Before commissioning an expensive pentest, run OWASP ZAP and Nessus Community Edition against your systems — both are free and catch the most common vulnerabilities. Address what they find first; a professional audit is worth it once the low-hanging fruit is gone.
We want to add automated end-to-end testing. A SaaS testing service costs $200/month.

Playwright and Cypress are both open-source and free. Setting them up takes some engineering time, but once done, the marginal cost is zero — paying a SaaS for this makes no sense when mature free tools exist.
The office is looking bare. Can we buy some plants and artwork to liven it up? Budget request is $500.

Cuttings from existing plants are free — ask around, plenty of people have pothos or succulents that propagate easily. For artwork, printing high-resolution public domain images at a drugstore costs under $5 each and looks great framed.
Our printer is broken. Repair quote is $150, but a new one is $200. Should we just buy a new one?

Repair it. A $50 difference is not worth the e-waste or the time spent setting up a new device. Also worth asking: how much do you actually print? If it's rarely used, this might be a good moment to go fully digital.
We need company swag for the upcoming conference — branded T-shirts, mugs, and tote bags for 100 people.

Swag almost always ends up in a drawer or a landfill within months. If you do go ahead, skip the mugs and tote bags and just do T-shirts — it's the only item people reliably keep. Order in bulk from a local screen printer to keep costs down.
But we want to make a good impression at the conference.

A well-designed, useful single item makes a better impression than a bag of forgettable trinkets. One quality T-shirt per person, ordered in bulk, will cost less and people will actually wear it — that's free walking advertising.
Can we hire a professional photographer for the company retreat?

Someone on the team almost certainly has a decent camera or a recent smartphone with portrait mode — designate them as the unofficial photographer for the day. Professional photos are great for product launches and headshots, not casual retreats.
We want to buy Adobe Creative Cloud for the whole marketing team. It's $55/user/month times 6 people.

That's nearly $4,000 a year. Canva's free tier covers most marketing design needs, and if they need vector work, Inkscape is free and powerful. Identify exactly which Adobe features they actually use before spending that.
Should we pay for a premium LinkedIn Recruiter account to find candidates? It's $800/month.

Post the role publicly on LinkedIn for free, cross-post to Hacker News' monthly 'Who's hiring' thread, and email your professional network. These free channels fill most roles before you ever need to pay for recruiter tools.
We need to buy Microsoft Office licenses for new employees.

Google Workspace is significantly cheaper and covers email, docs, sheets, and slides. If you're already paying for Workspace, don't add a separate Office subscription on top of it — people can export to .docx when needed.
The team wants the Slack paid plan to unlock message history beyond 90 days.

Before paying, ask whether you actually need to search messages older than 90 days in practice. Most teams don't. If there are specific things worth preserving, export and archive them to Google Drive before they expire.
But we've lost important context a few times because of the message limit.

The fix for that is documenting decisions in a shared doc or wiki at the time they're made — that's a habit change, not a paid plan. Slack history is a crutch that doesn't solve the underlying documentation problem.
We're considering paying for a business phone number service. It's $25/month.
Google Voice gives you a free business phone number with call forwarding and voicemail. For most small teams, it does everything a paid service does at zero cost.
Should we buy a whiteboard for the conference room? The nice ones are $400.
A roll of whiteboard contact paper from Amazon is $20 and turns any smooth wall into a writable surface. It works just as well for brainstorming sessions as a freestanding whiteboard.
We want to run a customer survey and are looking at SurveyMonkey's paid plan at $40/month.
Google Forms is completely free and handles unlimited questions and responses. For most customer surveys, the feature difference between it and a paid tool is negligible.
The dev team wants to use a managed Redis service. It's $50/month.
Redis Cloud and Railway both offer free tiers. Start there — $50/month for a managed cache is a cost worth delaying until traffic actually justifies it.
We need to renew our antivirus software license. It's $300/year for the team.

Windows Defender is built into Windows, maintained by Microsoft, and consistently rates among the top performers in independent tests. For most business users, there's no need to pay for third-party antivirus.
Can we buy standing desks for the whole office? About $500 each, 20 desks.

That's $10,000. Rather than outfitting everyone at once, get a few and let people share or rotate. Survey who actually wants one — demand is usually lower than you'd expect once people realize they have to assemble it themselves.
We need a project tracking tool. The team is leaning toward Jira at $8.15/user/month.

Linear and Trello both have free tiers that are genuinely usable. GitHub Issues is also built into your existing code repository at no extra cost. Exhaust these before adding another SaaS subscription.
Should we subscribe to an email marketing platform? Mailchimp's paid plan is $60/month.

Mailchimp's free plan supports up to 500 contacts and 1,000 emails per month — that covers most early-stage lists. Stay on the free plan until you genuinely hit the limits, not just because the paid features look appealing.
We need to print 500 brochures for an event. The design agency quoted $1,200 for design plus print.

Design the brochure yourself in Canva using a free template — it takes an afternoon and produces professional results. Then send the file to an online printer like Vistaprint; 500 brochures will cost under $100.
We're considering upgrading our CRM to the enterprise tier for the forecasting features. It's $150/user/month.

Before upgrading, check what forecasting data the team actually looks at today. If they aren't consistently using the CRM's basic features, adding an expensive tier won't change behavior — it'll just increase the bill.
The design team is requesting a Figma organization plan at $45/user/month.

Figma's professional plan at $12/user/month covers unlimited projects and version history, which is what most teams actually need. The organization tier is for large enterprises managing multiple teams — are you sure you need that tier?
We want to subscribe to a market research report. It's $2,000 for access.

Check if any of that research is publicly available through industry associations, academic institutions, or government data sources first. Statista has some free summaries too. $2,000 for a report that may be partly available for free is worth investigating before purchasing.
Should we pay for an SSL certificate upgrade? The EV certificate is $300/year.

EV certificates no longer display the green bar in modern browsers — the visual trust signal they used to provide is gone. A standard certificate from Let's Encrypt is free and provides the same encryption. There's no practical reason to pay $300 for this.
We're considering buying a 4K display for the main conference room. It's $700.

Does the current display have a functional problem, or is this an upgrade for aesthetics? A 1080p display is perfectly legible for presentations in any normal conference room. Save the $700 unless there's a specific, demonstrated need.
We want to commission custom illustrations for the website redesign.

Undraw.co and Humaaans offer free, polished illustrations you can customize to match your brand colors. For most websites, these are indistinguishable from custom work in terms of conversion or perception.
The HR team wants to use a learning management system for internal training. It's $8/user/month.

A shared Google Drive folder with organized training documents, Loom videos for walkthroughs, and a Google Form for knowledge checks replicates most LMS functionality for free. Buy software when the manual version breaks down, not before.
We need a CDN for our website. CloudFront and Fastly both have usage-based pricing.

Cloudflare's free plan includes a CDN with unlimited bandwidth and it's genuinely one of the best in the industry. For almost all websites and apps, there's no reason to pay for a CDN when Cloudflare offers this for free.
Should we pay for a professional voiceover for our product demo video?
Record it yourself with a decent USB microphone — the Blue Yeti Nano is $50 and produces professional-quality audio. A natural, authentic voice often converts better than a polished voiceover anyway.
Can we rent a coworking space for the team one day a week? It's $500/month.

Many public libraries now have free meeting rooms you can book for professional use. Coffee shops work too. $500/month is $6,000/year — worth exploring free alternatives first, especially if it's only one day a week.
We want to use Webflow for our marketing site. The CMS plan is $23/month.

Jekyll or Hugo are free static site generators that host on GitHub Pages or Netlify at zero cost. If the team is comfortable with a small amount of markdown, this covers most marketing site needs without any monthly fee.
But we don't have developers — our marketers maintain the site.

In that case, $23/month for Webflow is actually reasonable — it's purpose-built for non-developers. Just make sure the team actually uses it actively; subscriptions for infrequently updated sites are a quiet ongoing cost.
We need to buy new office headsets for customer support. Good ones are $150 each.

Anker and Mpow make USB headsets in the $25-40 range with very good microphone quality for call center work. The $150 options are often for audiophile use cases — the audio quality difference is imperceptible to customers.
We're thinking about hiring a PR agency. Retainer would be $5,000/month.

Before paying a monthly retainer, identify 20 journalists who cover your space and email them directly with a clear, specific story angle. This takes a day of research and costs nothing. PR agencies earn their fees at scale; most early-stage companies get better ROI from direct outreach.
We want to add a live chat widget to the website. Intercom starts at $74/month.

Tawk.to is a full-featured live chat platform that is completely free — they monetize through optional paid agent services, but the software itself costs nothing. It handles everything Intercom does for basic chat use cases.
Should we subscribe to a premium news aggregator for competitive intelligence? It's $30/month.

Set up free Google Alerts for your competitors' names, key industry terms, and your own brand. RSS feeds from industry blogs via Feedly's free tier cover most competitive news. $30/month for a news aggregator is easy to cut.
The engineering team wants GitHub Copilot licenses. It's $19/user/month per developer.

With 10 developers that's $2,280/year. Pilot it with 2-3 people for a month first to measure whether it actually increases output before rolling it out to everyone. Productivity tools that sound great often see lower-than-expected real-world usage.
We piloted it and the two developers who used it say they really like it.

Liking a tool and measurably increasing output are different things. Ask them to estimate concrete time saved per day — if it's more than 30 minutes each, the math works out. If it's primarily a quality-of-life improvement, weigh that against cost and decide deliberately.
We need to buy a domain for a new internal tool. The .com is taken, so it's $2,000 on the aftermarket.

For an internal tool, use a subdomain on your existing company domain — something like tools.yourcompany.com costs nothing. You don't need a separate domain, let alone a $2,000 one, for something only employees will access.
Can we get a paid Calendly plan for scheduling? It's $10/month.

Calendly's free plan covers one event type and that's enough for most people's scheduling needs. Cal.com is a fully-featured open-source alternative with a free tier that includes multiple event types. Worth trying before paying.
We want to run a referral program and need software to track it. Options start at $50/month.

A referral program can be run on a spreadsheet with a unique coupon code per referrer. Track it in Sheets for free until you're handling enough volume that manual tracking becomes genuinely time-consuming — that's the point at which $50/month becomes worth it.
We're running low on Google Drive storage. Should we upgrade the plan? It's $10/month for 2TB.

Before upgrading, go through what's stored and delete or archive old files. Most storage issues come from never cleaning up, not from genuinely needing more space. A two-hour cleanup session is free and usually solves it.
We want to translate our app into 5 additional languages. Professional translation is quoted at $0.15/word.

Run the strings through DeepL first and have a native speaker in your network do a review pass for each language. Many people will do a 30-minute review of a UI string file as a favor. Save professional translation for content where nuance is legally or commercially critical.
Can we fly our remote employees in for an all-hands? Flights and hotels for 12 people — probably $15,000.

Is there a way to hold the all-hands virtually with a high-quality video setup this quarter and save the in-person gathering for when there's a strategic moment that specifically benefits from everyone being in the room together?
We need a dedicated status page for our service. Statuspage.io starts at $29/month.
Freshstatus offers a free hosted status page, and Upptime runs entirely on GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for free. There's no need to pay for a status page — several excellent free solutions exist.
We want to outsource our social media management to an agency. They quoted $2,500/month.

Designate someone internally to own social for 2-3 hours a week, use Buffer's free plan to schedule posts, and repurpose content you're already creating. $2,500/month is a significant spend for a channel where authentic, consistent posting beats agency-produced content most of the time anyway.
Should we buy a SaaS spend management tool to track all our subscriptions? It's $25/month.

The irony of paying for a tool to track your spending is real. A Google Sheet with columns for tool name, cost, billing cycle, and owner takes 30 minutes to set up and does the same job for free. Review it quarterly.
We want to hire a video editor to produce our monthly product update videos.

DaVinci Resolve is a professional-grade video editor that's completely free. If someone on the team can spend a few hours learning the basics, you can produce clean, polished update videos without paying a freelancer every month.
We're considering buying an office coffee subscription service — fresh beans delivered monthly. It's $80/month.

A large bag of decent ground coffee from Costco costs about $12 and lasts weeks. The subscription premium buys marginally better taste that most people won't notice once they're three sips into a Monday morning.
Should we pay for a premium Grammarly business plan for the team at $25/user/month?

The free version of Grammarly catches the vast majority of errors. Microsoft Word and Google Docs also have built-in grammar checkers that most people underuse. Try the free tools consistently before paying $25/user for marginal improvements.
Can we get professional headshots done for all employees? A photographer quoted $1,500 for the whole team.

Set up a phone on a tripod in front of a plain white wall, use portrait mode, and edit with a free app like Snapseed. For LinkedIn photos, the difference between that and a $1,500 shoot is much smaller than you'd think.
We want to add a knowledge base for customers. Zendesk Guide costs $55/agent/month.

Notion has a free plan that supports public-facing pages you can organize as a knowledge base. GitBook also offers a free tier for open documentation. There's no need to pay Zendesk rates for a help center.
The team is asking for a subscription to a generative AI image tool for presentations. It's $30/month.

Microsoft Designer is free with a Microsoft account and generates presentation-quality images. Google Slides has AI image generation built in too. Exhaust the free tools before adding another subscription.
We need to send 200 direct mail pieces to prospects. A mailing service quoted $600.

Email the same prospects first — it costs nothing and you'll learn which messages resonate before spending $600 on physical mail. Direct mail makes sense as a follow-up to warm leads, not a cold first touch.
Should we upgrade our video conferencing setup with a $800 conference room camera?

A $60 Logitech webcam on a good mount does the job for most meeting rooms. The diminishing returns on camera hardware above $100 are steep — unless you're running broadcast-quality webinars, this is hard to justify.
We want to hire an executive coach for our leadership team. Sessions are $400/hour.

There's a huge library of leadership books, free Harvard Business Review articles, and podcast interviews with experienced executives. Start there. If you identify a specific gap after six months of self-directed learning, a few targeted coaching sessions might be worth it.
Can we subscribe to a team wellness app? It's $6/employee/month.

Headspace and Calm both have free content. The NHS also publishes free mental health resources. Before paying a per-employee subscription, check whether the free tiers of existing apps actually cover the use cases you have in mind.
We need to print name badges and lanyards for our event. Vendor quoted $400 for 100 people.

Print name badge inserts on a standard office printer and buy blank badge holders and lanyards in bulk on Amazon — you'll come in under $50 for 100 people. The vendor is charging mostly for convenience.
We're thinking of getting an office cleaning service. Quote is $300/week.

Set up a rotating cleaning schedule among the team for shared spaces and common areas. A weekly shared responsibility for tidying the kitchen and bathrooms takes five minutes per person and keeps the cost at zero.
Should we pay for a professional audio transcription service for our meeting notes? It's $0.25/minute.

Otter.ai has a generous free plan that automatically transcribes meetings in real time. Google Meet and Zoom also include built-in transcription at no additional cost on standard plans. There's no need to pay per-minute for transcription.
We want to set up an internal wiki and are looking at Confluence. It's $5.75/user/month.

Notion's free plan supports up to 10 guests and unlimited pages, and Outline is completely open-source and self-hostable. For a small team, either option costs nothing and is just as searchable as Confluence.
Can we use a paid appointment scheduling tool for client bookings? It's $20/month.
Calendly's free plan allows one event type, which is enough for most individual booking use cases. If you need more types, Cal.com is open-source with no monthly fee. Test the free options first.
We want to offer employees a stipend for home office setup. $500 per person.

If employees are already working from home effectively, a stipend is a nice-to-have rather than a necessity. If there are specific productivity issues, identify them first — sometimes the solution is a free monitor positioning guide, not a cash outlay.
We need to buy props and decorations for the office holiday party. Budget is $400.
Dollar stores and party discount shops have extensive holiday decoration sections. For $50 you can make a space look genuinely festive — you don't need $400 of branded props for a one-evening party.
Should we hire a UX writer to improve our app microcopy?

Read the book 'Strategic Writing for UX' — it's under $20 and gives whoever owns the product the framework to rewrite the copy themselves. Hiring a specialist for microcopy makes sense at scale; at this stage, internal iteration is cheaper and faster.
We want to send gift cards to survey respondents as an incentive. $25 each, 200 respondents.

That's $5,000. Many surveys get strong response rates with no incentive when the subject matter is relevant to the respondent. Try sending the survey without incentives first to your warmest contacts before committing to paid incentives.
The ops team wants a dedicated VPN service for the company. It's $8/user/month.
Cloudflare WARP is free and provides encrypted DNS and basic VPN functionality. For most small teams, it covers the security needs without a per-user subscription fee.
We're planning to redo the office signage and logo walls. Designer quoted $1,800.

Vinyl lettering from a local sign shop is a fraction of the cost and looks clean and professional. You design the layout in Canva for free, send them the file, and they cut and install it for under $200 in most cities.
Can we buy noise-canceling headphones for everyone in the open office? They're $300 each.

Sony and Anker make noise-canceling headphones in the $50-80 range that independent reviewers consistently rate nearly as highly as the flagship models. The $300 pair buys marginally better noise cancellation that most people won't notice after the first week.
We want to use a third-party service to monitor our website uptime. Plans start at $20/month.
UptimeRobot has a free plan that monitors up to 50 URLs and alerts you within 5 minutes of downtime. For most websites, that's more than sufficient and costs nothing.
Should we purchase a premium weather API for our logistics app? It's $200/month.

Open-Meteo provides free weather API access with no API key required, and the National Weather Service offers free data in the US. Test whether free sources meet your accuracy and coverage needs before paying $200/month.
We need a shared inbox tool for customer email. Front charges $19/user/month.

A shared Gmail account with labels, canned responses, and clear assignment conventions handles team email effectively at no extra cost. Shared inbox tools earn their fee at high volumes — most small teams don't need the overhead.
We want to run a virtual trivia night for the remote team. Event companies charge $500 for a hosted session.

Kahoot has a free tier and you can build a trivia game in 30 minutes. Assign one person to host it on a video call and run it yourselves. $500 for something you can do for free with a bit of prep time is hard to justify.
Should we subscribe to a podcast hosting platform? Plans start at $19/month.

Spotify for Podcasters (formerly Anchor) provides free hosting, analytics, and distribution to all major platforms. There's no reason to pay for podcast hosting until you have a very specific feature need that free platforms don't cover.
We need to buy a label printer for shipping. A decent one is $200.

How many shipments are you actually sending per week? If it's fewer than 20, printing labels on a standard inkjet and using standard tape is perfectly serviceable. A dedicated label printer pays for itself only at meaningful shipping volume.
Can we pay for a premium mapping API? Google Maps charges per request above the free tier.

OpenStreetMap with the Leaflet library is completely free and handles most mapping use cases. If you need geocoding, Nominatim is free. Exhaust the open-source mapping ecosystem before paying Google's per-request pricing.
We're thinking about buying ergonomic chair mats for everyone's home offices.

This is a nice gesture but not a business necessity. If employees want one, a $20 plastic mat from Amazon solves the problem. Purchasing these centrally and shipping them to everyone adds cost and logistics overhead that outweighs the benefit.

Before spending $500, post the relevant sections on code review communities like Stack Overflow or ask in a relevant Discord server — experienced engineers often give thorough feedback for free. Alternatively, swap reviews with a peer company.
We need to cater lunch for an all-hands meeting with 40 people.
Costco or a warehouse club is the way to go — sandwich platters and drinks for 40 people will run you a third of what a catering company charges for the same spread.
Our designer wants to purchase a premium font license for the rebrand. It's $400.

Google Fonts has over 1,400 free, professionally designed typefaces and many top brands use them. Unless there's a very specific reason the rebrand requires that exact font, we should design around free options.
We have a contract with a new vendor and legal suggested we get a lawyer to review it.

For a standard vendor contract, try running it through a free tool like a contract template checklist to flag obvious issues yourself first. Reserve the lawyer for anything that looks genuinely unusual.
But what if we miss something important?

Focus on the three things that actually matter in most vendor contracts: payment terms, liability caps, and termination clauses. If all three look standard, the risk of skipping a full legal review on a routine contract is low and saving $300-500 is worth it.
We need to translate our website into Spanish and French. Should we hire a translation agency?

Start with DeepL — it's significantly better than Google Translate and free for reasonable volumes. Have a native-speaking colleague do a quick pass to catch any awkward phrasing, which costs nothing.
Our current backup solution is almost full. The upgrade is $50/month.

Before upgrading, go through what's being backed up and delete redundant or outdated files. Most backup bloat comes from old logs and duplicate data. Cleaning house first is free and might solve the problem entirely.
Several employees are asking for ergonomic keyboard and mouse sets. Each one costs about $120.

Check if there are unused peripherals elsewhere in the office first — people hoard equipment. For the remainder, generic ergonomic keyboards on Amazon run $25-40 and do the same job; the brand-name premium is mostly marketing.
HR wants to organize a team-building escape room for 20 people. It's $800.

There are free team-building activities that are just as engaging — a trivia competition, a cooking challenge with pantry ingredients, or a group problem-solving exercise costs nothing and often sparks better conversations than a scripted escape room.
We want to run paid Google Ads to promote the new product launch. Starting budget is $5,000.

Before committing $5,000, exhaust the free channels first: post in relevant Reddit communities, reach out to journalists for coverage, and send a launch email to your existing list. Paid ads make sense once you've validated messaging with zero spend.
Should we hire a copywriter to redo our website copy? Quotes are coming in around $2,000.

Look at the websites of two or three competitors you admire and study how they describe their value proposition. Then rewrite your own copy modeling that structure — it's free and you understand your product better than any copywriter will after a brief.
We need to ship 50 sample boxes to potential clients. Standard shipping vs. expedited — should we pay for faster delivery?
Standard shipping. Unless there's a hard deadline tied to a specific meeting or event, paying extra for speed on a sales sample is hard to justify — clients aren't going anywhere.
The team wants to upgrade from Zoom free to the paid plan at $15/user/month.

What's the actual problem you're trying to solve? If it's the 40-minute meeting limit, you can simply rejoin the call for free. If it's something else, let's look at whether Google Meet covers it — it's already included in the Workspace subscription.
We need onboarding software to streamline the new hire process. The cheapest option is $8/employee/month.

A well-structured Notion or Google Sites page with a clear checklist costs nothing and works perfectly well for most teams under 50 people. Build the process first; buy software to automate it only when the manual version is already working well.
We're considering a dedicated analytics dashboard tool like Tableau. It's $70/user/month.

Google Looker Studio is free and connects directly to Google Sheets, BigQuery, and most data sources. For most reporting needs, it's indistinguishable from Tableau for a fraction — actually zero — of the cost.
Our web host is suggesting we upgrade to a dedicated server for better performance. It's $200/month vs. $20 now.

A tenfold price increase needs a very clear justification. Pull your actual traffic and load metrics first — shared hosting handles the vast majority of sites just fine, and if there are specific performance issues, a caching layer or CDN often fixes them for free.
The office internet has been slow. IT is suggesting we upgrade our bandwidth package — it's an extra $150/month.

Before adding bandwidth, check whether someone is running a large backup or sync job during business hours — that's usually the culprit. Also confirm the router firmware is up to date. These fixes are free and solve it more often than not.
Should we offer gym memberships as an employee benefit? About $40/person/month.

A lot of employees won't use it regularly, and you'd be paying for memberships whether they go or not. Sharing a curated list of free workout YouTube channels, local running clubs, or free city park programs is an alternative that costs nothing.
We're thinking about outsourcing our bookkeeping to an accounting firm. Their quote is $800/month.

Wave Accounting is completely free and handles invoicing, expense tracking, and basic reporting well. Pair it with a tidy chart of accounts and a monthly reconciliation habit, and you won't need to pay anyone for routine bookkeeping.
Our CTO wants to pay for a professional penetration test. The quote is $8,000.

Before commissioning an expensive pentest, run OWASP ZAP and Nessus Community Edition against your systems — both are free and catch the most common vulnerabilities. Address what they find first; a professional audit is worth it once the low-hanging fruit is gone.
We want to add automated end-to-end testing. A SaaS testing service costs $200/month.

Playwright and Cypress are both open-source and free. Setting them up takes some engineering time, but once done, the marginal cost is zero — paying a SaaS for this makes no sense when mature free tools exist.
The office is looking bare. Can we buy some plants and artwork to liven it up? Budget request is $500.

Cuttings from existing plants are free — ask around, plenty of people have pothos or succulents that propagate easily. For artwork, printing high-resolution public domain images at a drugstore costs under $5 each and looks great framed.
Our printer is broken. Repair quote is $150, but a new one is $200. Should we just buy a new one?

Repair it. A $50 difference is not worth the e-waste or the time spent setting up a new device. Also worth asking: how much do you actually print? If it's rarely used, this might be a good moment to go fully digital.
We need company swag for the upcoming conference — branded T-shirts, mugs, and tote bags for 100 people.

Swag almost always ends up in a drawer or a landfill within months. If you do go ahead, skip the mugs and tote bags and just do T-shirts — it's the only item people reliably keep. Order in bulk from a local screen printer to keep costs down.
But we want to make a good impression at the conference.

A well-designed, useful single item makes a better impression than a bag of forgettable trinkets. One quality T-shirt per person, ordered in bulk, will cost less and people will actually wear it — that's free walking advertising.
Can we hire a professional photographer for the company retreat?

Someone on the team almost certainly has a decent camera or a recent smartphone with portrait mode — designate them as the unofficial photographer for the day. Professional photos are great for product launches and headshots, not casual retreats.
We want to buy Adobe Creative Cloud for the whole marketing team. It's $55/user/month times 6 people.

That's nearly $4,000 a year. Canva's free tier covers most marketing design needs, and if they need vector work, Inkscape is free and powerful. Identify exactly which Adobe features they actually use before spending that.
Should we pay for a premium LinkedIn Recruiter account to find candidates? It's $800/month.

Post the role publicly on LinkedIn for free, cross-post to Hacker News' monthly 'Who's hiring' thread, and email your professional network. These free channels fill most roles before you ever need to pay for recruiter tools.
We need to buy Microsoft Office licenses for new employees.

Google Workspace is significantly cheaper and covers email, docs, sheets, and slides. If you're already paying for Workspace, don't add a separate Office subscription on top of it — people can export to .docx when needed.
The team wants the Slack paid plan to unlock message history beyond 90 days.

Before paying, ask whether you actually need to search messages older than 90 days in practice. Most teams don't. If there are specific things worth preserving, export and archive them to Google Drive before they expire.
But we've lost important context a few times because of the message limit.

The fix for that is documenting decisions in a shared doc or wiki at the time they're made — that's a habit change, not a paid plan. Slack history is a crutch that doesn't solve the underlying documentation problem.
We're considering paying for a business phone number service. It's $25/month.
Google Voice gives you a free business phone number with call forwarding and voicemail. For most small teams, it does everything a paid service does at zero cost.
Should we buy a whiteboard for the conference room? The nice ones are $400.
A roll of whiteboard contact paper from Amazon is $20 and turns any smooth wall into a writable surface. It works just as well for brainstorming sessions as a freestanding whiteboard.
We want to run a customer survey and are looking at SurveyMonkey's paid plan at $40/month.
Google Forms is completely free and handles unlimited questions and responses. For most customer surveys, the feature difference between it and a paid tool is negligible.
The dev team wants to use a managed Redis service. It's $50/month.
Redis Cloud and Railway both offer free tiers. Start there — $50/month for a managed cache is a cost worth delaying until traffic actually justifies it.
We need to renew our antivirus software license. It's $300/year for the team.

Windows Defender is built into Windows, maintained by Microsoft, and consistently rates among the top performers in independent tests. For most business users, there's no need to pay for third-party antivirus.
Can we buy standing desks for the whole office? About $500 each, 20 desks.

That's $10,000. Rather than outfitting everyone at once, get a few and let people share or rotate. Survey who actually wants one — demand is usually lower than you'd expect once people realize they have to assemble it themselves.
We need a project tracking tool. The team is leaning toward Jira at $8.15/user/month.

Linear and Trello both have free tiers that are genuinely usable. GitHub Issues is also built into your existing code repository at no extra cost. Exhaust these before adding another SaaS subscription.
Should we subscribe to an email marketing platform? Mailchimp's paid plan is $60/month.

Mailchimp's free plan supports up to 500 contacts and 1,000 emails per month — that covers most early-stage lists. Stay on the free plan until you genuinely hit the limits, not just because the paid features look appealing.
We need to print 500 brochures for an event. The design agency quoted $1,200 for design plus print.

Design the brochure yourself in Canva using a free template — it takes an afternoon and produces professional results. Then send the file to an online printer like Vistaprint; 500 brochures will cost under $100.
We're considering upgrading our CRM to the enterprise tier for the forecasting features. It's $150/user/month.

Before upgrading, check what forecasting data the team actually looks at today. If they aren't consistently using the CRM's basic features, adding an expensive tier won't change behavior — it'll just increase the bill.
The design team is requesting a Figma organization plan at $45/user/month.

Figma's professional plan at $12/user/month covers unlimited projects and version history, which is what most teams actually need. The organization tier is for large enterprises managing multiple teams — are you sure you need that tier?
We want to subscribe to a market research report. It's $2,000 for access.

Check if any of that research is publicly available through industry associations, academic institutions, or government data sources first. Statista has some free summaries too. $2,000 for a report that may be partly available for free is worth investigating before purchasing.
Should we pay for an SSL certificate upgrade? The EV certificate is $300/year.

EV certificates no longer display the green bar in modern browsers — the visual trust signal they used to provide is gone. A standard certificate from Let's Encrypt is free and provides the same encryption. There's no practical reason to pay $300 for this.
We're considering buying a 4K display for the main conference room. It's $700.

Does the current display have a functional problem, or is this an upgrade for aesthetics? A 1080p display is perfectly legible for presentations in any normal conference room. Save the $700 unless there's a specific, demonstrated need.
We want to commission custom illustrations for the website redesign.

Undraw.co and Humaaans offer free, polished illustrations you can customize to match your brand colors. For most websites, these are indistinguishable from custom work in terms of conversion or perception.
The HR team wants to use a learning management system for internal training. It's $8/user/month.

A shared Google Drive folder with organized training documents, Loom videos for walkthroughs, and a Google Form for knowledge checks replicates most LMS functionality for free. Buy software when the manual version breaks down, not before.
We need a CDN for our website. CloudFront and Fastly both have usage-based pricing.

Cloudflare's free plan includes a CDN with unlimited bandwidth and it's genuinely one of the best in the industry. For almost all websites and apps, there's no reason to pay for a CDN when Cloudflare offers this for free.
Should we pay for a professional voiceover for our product demo video?
Record it yourself with a decent USB microphone — the Blue Yeti Nano is $50 and produces professional-quality audio. A natural, authentic voice often converts better than a polished voiceover anyway.
Can we rent a coworking space for the team one day a week? It's $500/month.

Many public libraries now have free meeting rooms you can book for professional use. Coffee shops work too. $500/month is $6,000/year — worth exploring free alternatives first, especially if it's only one day a week.
We want to use Webflow for our marketing site. The CMS plan is $23/month.

Jekyll or Hugo are free static site generators that host on GitHub Pages or Netlify at zero cost. If the team is comfortable with a small amount of markdown, this covers most marketing site needs without any monthly fee.
But we don't have developers — our marketers maintain the site.

In that case, $23/month for Webflow is actually reasonable — it's purpose-built for non-developers. Just make sure the team actually uses it actively; subscriptions for infrequently updated sites are a quiet ongoing cost.
We need to buy new office headsets for customer support. Good ones are $150 each.

Anker and Mpow make USB headsets in the $25-40 range with very good microphone quality for call center work. The $150 options are often for audiophile use cases — the audio quality difference is imperceptible to customers.
We're thinking about hiring a PR agency. Retainer would be $5,000/month.

Before paying a monthly retainer, identify 20 journalists who cover your space and email them directly with a clear, specific story angle. This takes a day of research and costs nothing. PR agencies earn their fees at scale; most early-stage companies get better ROI from direct outreach.
We want to add a live chat widget to the website. Intercom starts at $74/month.

Tawk.to is a full-featured live chat platform that is completely free — they monetize through optional paid agent services, but the software itself costs nothing. It handles everything Intercom does for basic chat use cases.
Should we subscribe to a premium news aggregator for competitive intelligence? It's $30/month.

Set up free Google Alerts for your competitors' names, key industry terms, and your own brand. RSS feeds from industry blogs via Feedly's free tier cover most competitive news. $30/month for a news aggregator is easy to cut.
The engineering team wants GitHub Copilot licenses. It's $19/user/month per developer.

With 10 developers that's $2,280/year. Pilot it with 2-3 people for a month first to measure whether it actually increases output before rolling it out to everyone. Productivity tools that sound great often see lower-than-expected real-world usage.
We piloted it and the two developers who used it say they really like it.

Liking a tool and measurably increasing output are different things. Ask them to estimate concrete time saved per day — if it's more than 30 minutes each, the math works out. If it's primarily a quality-of-life improvement, weigh that against cost and decide deliberately.
We need to buy a domain for a new internal tool. The .com is taken, so it's $2,000 on the aftermarket.

For an internal tool, use a subdomain on your existing company domain — something like tools.yourcompany.com costs nothing. You don't need a separate domain, let alone a $2,000 one, for something only employees will access.
Can we get a paid Calendly plan for scheduling? It's $10/month.

Calendly's free plan covers one event type and that's enough for most people's scheduling needs. Cal.com is a fully-featured open-source alternative with a free tier that includes multiple event types. Worth trying before paying.
We want to run a referral program and need software to track it. Options start at $50/month.

A referral program can be run on a spreadsheet with a unique coupon code per referrer. Track it in Sheets for free until you're handling enough volume that manual tracking becomes genuinely time-consuming — that's the point at which $50/month becomes worth it.
We're running low on Google Drive storage. Should we upgrade the plan? It's $10/month for 2TB.

Before upgrading, go through what's stored and delete or archive old files. Most storage issues come from never cleaning up, not from genuinely needing more space. A two-hour cleanup session is free and usually solves it.
We want to translate our app into 5 additional languages. Professional translation is quoted at $0.15/word.

Run the strings through DeepL first and have a native speaker in your network do a review pass for each language. Many people will do a 30-minute review of a UI string file as a favor. Save professional translation for content where nuance is legally or commercially critical.
Can we fly our remote employees in for an all-hands? Flights and hotels for 12 people — probably $15,000.

Is there a way to hold the all-hands virtually with a high-quality video setup this quarter and save the in-person gathering for when there's a strategic moment that specifically benefits from everyone being in the room together?
We need a dedicated status page for our service. Statuspage.io starts at $29/month.
Freshstatus offers a free hosted status page, and Upptime runs entirely on GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for free. There's no need to pay for a status page — several excellent free solutions exist.
We want to outsource our social media management to an agency. They quoted $2,500/month.

Designate someone internally to own social for 2-3 hours a week, use Buffer's free plan to schedule posts, and repurpose content you're already creating. $2,500/month is a significant spend for a channel where authentic, consistent posting beats agency-produced content most of the time anyway.
Should we buy a SaaS spend management tool to track all our subscriptions? It's $25/month.

The irony of paying for a tool to track your spending is real. A Google Sheet with columns for tool name, cost, billing cycle, and owner takes 30 minutes to set up and does the same job for free. Review it quarterly.
We want to hire a video editor to produce our monthly product update videos.

DaVinci Resolve is a professional-grade video editor that's completely free. If someone on the team can spend a few hours learning the basics, you can produce clean, polished update videos without paying a freelancer every month.
We're considering buying an office coffee subscription service — fresh beans delivered monthly. It's $80/month.

A large bag of decent ground coffee from Costco costs about $12 and lasts weeks. The subscription premium buys marginally better taste that most people won't notice once they're three sips into a Monday morning.
Should we pay for a premium Grammarly business plan for the team at $25/user/month?

The free version of Grammarly catches the vast majority of errors. Microsoft Word and Google Docs also have built-in grammar checkers that most people underuse. Try the free tools consistently before paying $25/user for marginal improvements.
Can we get professional headshots done for all employees? A photographer quoted $1,500 for the whole team.

Set up a phone on a tripod in front of a plain white wall, use portrait mode, and edit with a free app like Snapseed. For LinkedIn photos, the difference between that and a $1,500 shoot is much smaller than you'd think.
We want to add a knowledge base for customers. Zendesk Guide costs $55/agent/month.

Notion has a free plan that supports public-facing pages you can organize as a knowledge base. GitBook also offers a free tier for open documentation. There's no need to pay Zendesk rates for a help center.
The team is asking for a subscription to a generative AI image tool for presentations. It's $30/month.

Microsoft Designer is free with a Microsoft account and generates presentation-quality images. Google Slides has AI image generation built in too. Exhaust the free tools before adding another subscription.
We need to send 200 direct mail pieces to prospects. A mailing service quoted $600.

Email the same prospects first — it costs nothing and you'll learn which messages resonate before spending $600 on physical mail. Direct mail makes sense as a follow-up to warm leads, not a cold first touch.
Should we upgrade our video conferencing setup with a $800 conference room camera?

A $60 Logitech webcam on a good mount does the job for most meeting rooms. The diminishing returns on camera hardware above $100 are steep — unless you're running broadcast-quality webinars, this is hard to justify.
We want to hire an executive coach for our leadership team. Sessions are $400/hour.

There's a huge library of leadership books, free Harvard Business Review articles, and podcast interviews with experienced executives. Start there. If you identify a specific gap after six months of self-directed learning, a few targeted coaching sessions might be worth it.
Can we subscribe to a team wellness app? It's $6/employee/month.

Headspace and Calm both have free content. The NHS also publishes free mental health resources. Before paying a per-employee subscription, check whether the free tiers of existing apps actually cover the use cases you have in mind.
We need to print name badges and lanyards for our event. Vendor quoted $400 for 100 people.

Print name badge inserts on a standard office printer and buy blank badge holders and lanyards in bulk on Amazon — you'll come in under $50 for 100 people. The vendor is charging mostly for convenience.
We're thinking of getting an office cleaning service. Quote is $300/week.

Set up a rotating cleaning schedule among the team for shared spaces and common areas. A weekly shared responsibility for tidying the kitchen and bathrooms takes five minutes per person and keeps the cost at zero.
Should we pay for a professional audio transcription service for our meeting notes? It's $0.25/minute.

Otter.ai has a generous free plan that automatically transcribes meetings in real time. Google Meet and Zoom also include built-in transcription at no additional cost on standard plans. There's no need to pay per-minute for transcription.
We want to set up an internal wiki and are looking at Confluence. It's $5.75/user/month.

Notion's free plan supports up to 10 guests and unlimited pages, and Outline is completely open-source and self-hostable. For a small team, either option costs nothing and is just as searchable as Confluence.
Can we use a paid appointment scheduling tool for client bookings? It's $20/month.
Calendly's free plan allows one event type, which is enough for most individual booking use cases. If you need more types, Cal.com is open-source with no monthly fee. Test the free options first.
We want to offer employees a stipend for home office setup. $500 per person.

If employees are already working from home effectively, a stipend is a nice-to-have rather than a necessity. If there are specific productivity issues, identify them first — sometimes the solution is a free monitor positioning guide, not a cash outlay.
We need to buy props and decorations for the office holiday party. Budget is $400.
Dollar stores and party discount shops have extensive holiday decoration sections. For $50 you can make a space look genuinely festive — you don't need $400 of branded props for a one-evening party.
Should we hire a UX writer to improve our app microcopy?

Read the book 'Strategic Writing for UX' — it's under $20 and gives whoever owns the product the framework to rewrite the copy themselves. Hiring a specialist for microcopy makes sense at scale; at this stage, internal iteration is cheaper and faster.
We want to send gift cards to survey respondents as an incentive. $25 each, 200 respondents.

That's $5,000. Many surveys get strong response rates with no incentive when the subject matter is relevant to the respondent. Try sending the survey without incentives first to your warmest contacts before committing to paid incentives.
The ops team wants a dedicated VPN service for the company. It's $8/user/month.
Cloudflare WARP is free and provides encrypted DNS and basic VPN functionality. For most small teams, it covers the security needs without a per-user subscription fee.
We're planning to redo the office signage and logo walls. Designer quoted $1,800.

Vinyl lettering from a local sign shop is a fraction of the cost and looks clean and professional. You design the layout in Canva for free, send them the file, and they cut and install it for under $200 in most cities.
Can we buy noise-canceling headphones for everyone in the open office? They're $300 each.

Sony and Anker make noise-canceling headphones in the $50-80 range that independent reviewers consistently rate nearly as highly as the flagship models. The $300 pair buys marginally better noise cancellation that most people won't notice after the first week.
We want to use a third-party service to monitor our website uptime. Plans start at $20/month.
UptimeRobot has a free plan that monitors up to 50 URLs and alerts you within 5 minutes of downtime. For most websites, that's more than sufficient and costs nothing.
Should we purchase a premium weather API for our logistics app? It's $200/month.

Open-Meteo provides free weather API access with no API key required, and the National Weather Service offers free data in the US. Test whether free sources meet your accuracy and coverage needs before paying $200/month.
We need a shared inbox tool for customer email. Front charges $19/user/month.

A shared Gmail account with labels, canned responses, and clear assignment conventions handles team email effectively at no extra cost. Shared inbox tools earn their fee at high volumes — most small teams don't need the overhead.
We want to run a virtual trivia night for the remote team. Event companies charge $500 for a hosted session.

Kahoot has a free tier and you can build a trivia game in 30 minutes. Assign one person to host it on a video call and run it yourselves. $500 for something you can do for free with a bit of prep time is hard to justify.
Should we subscribe to a podcast hosting platform? Plans start at $19/month.

Spotify for Podcasters (formerly Anchor) provides free hosting, analytics, and distribution to all major platforms. There's no reason to pay for podcast hosting until you have a very specific feature need that free platforms don't cover.
We need to buy a label printer for shipping. A decent one is $200.

How many shipments are you actually sending per week? If it's fewer than 20, printing labels on a standard inkjet and using standard tape is perfectly serviceable. A dedicated label printer pays for itself only at meaningful shipping volume.
Can we pay for a premium mapping API? Google Maps charges per request above the free tier.

OpenStreetMap with the Leaflet library is completely free and handles most mapping use cases. If you need geocoding, Nominatim is free. Exhaust the open-source mapping ecosystem before paying Google's per-request pricing.
We're thinking about buying ergonomic chair mats for everyone's home offices.

This is a nice gesture but not a business necessity. If employees want one, a $20 plastic mat from Amazon solves the problem. Purchasing these centrally and shipping them to everyone adds cost and logistics overhead that outweighs the benefit.
We're hitting the rate limits on the free API tier. Should we upgrade to the paid plan at $200/month?

Hold off on that. First, let's audit how we're actually using the API — there's a good chance we can reduce call frequency or cache responses to stay within the free tier. Have you looked at where the requests are coming from?
We need to rent a large format printer for the trade show next month.

Before renting, check whether a local print shop can produce what you need — they're almost always cheaper than renting the equipment yourself. If it's just a few banners, uploading a file and paying per print will cost a fraction of a rental.
I want to hire a data analyst to help us understand our sales trends.

Can you pull the data into a spreadsheet first and take a look yourself? Google Sheets has built-in pivot tables and charts that handle most trend analysis without any specialist. If you get stuck on something specific, that's a much cheaper one-hour consultation than a full hire.
Should we pay for a custom domain for our new project? It's only $12 a year.
For an internal or experimental project, a free subdomain on GitHub Pages or Netlify is perfectly fine. Wait until the project proves it has real traction before spending anything on a domain.
The team is asking for an espresso machine in the kitchen. A decent one is about $600.
Instant coffee and a $15 French press will cover 95% of what people actually need. A $600 machine also comes with maintenance costs and someone has to clean it — the hidden costs add up fast.
We want to send the engineering team to a React conference. Tickets are $800 each and there are 5 of them.
That's $4,000 before travel and hotel. The React team posts full conference talks on YouTube within weeks — you could run an internal watch party for free and get essentially the same content.
But they'd also get to network and ask questions live.
Networking is valuable, but $4,000 is a lot to spend on that. Could you send just one person as a representative and have them share notes with the rest of the team? That cuts the cost by 80%.
We're considering an A/B testing platform. The cheapest plan is $300/month.

At that price point, it's worth checking whether your analytics tool already has basic A/B testing built in — Google Optimize was free before it sunset, and tools like PostHog have generous free tiers. What volume of experiments are you actually planning to run?
The marketing team wants to buy a pack of premium stock photos. It's $49/month.
Unsplash, Pexels, and Pixabay have huge libraries of high-quality photos that are completely free with no attribution required. We should exhaust those options before paying for a subscription.

Before spending $500, post the relevant sections on code review communities like Stack Overflow or ask in a relevant Discord server — experienced engineers often give thorough feedback for free. Alternatively, swap reviews with a peer company.

Costco or a warehouse club is the way to go — sandwich platters and drinks for 40 people will run you a third of what a catering company charges for the same spread.

Google Fonts has over 1,400 free, professionally designed typefaces and many top brands use them. Unless there's a very specific reason the rebrand requires that exact font, we should design around free options.

But what if we miss something important?
